entry: Autocephalous [[Eastern Orthodox Church|Eastern Orthodox]] church headed by the Ecumenical Patriarch of [[Constantinople]]. The see holds special honor as the former capital of the Eastern Roman Empire and mother church of most modern Eastern Orthodox churches, and its Ecumenical Patriarch holds the status of *primus inter pares* (first among equals) among the world's Eastern Orthodox primates. In 330 AD, [[Constantine the Great]] moved his residence to the city, renaming it Nova Roma, and at the First Council of Constantinople in 381 the see was recognized as the fourth ancient patriarchate, after [[Antioch]], [[Alexandria]] and [[Rome]]. Its 2019 grant of autocephaly to the Orthodox Church of Ukraine led to schisms, including a break in communion with the [[Russian Orthodox Church]], which disputes the see's appellate authority. The reopening of the Theological School of Halki, closed by Turkish authorities in 1971, is a prominent 21st-century issue.

Principle that Christians of different denominations should cooperate toward closer relations and greater unity. The adjective *ecumenical* applies to any interdenominational initiative that promotes such cooperation, and ecumenists regard baptism and faith in Jesus as the basis of Christian unity, citing John 17:20–23. In 1920, the Ecumenical Patriarch of the Eastern Orthodox Church, Germanus V of Constantinople, urged closer cooperation among separated Christians and proposed a "League of Churches" parallel to the newly founded [[League of Nations]]. In 1937, Christian leaders resolved to establish the World Council of Churches, which today includes most major Christian traditions as full members, while the [[Catholic Church|Roman Catholic Church]] participates as an observer. Critics argue that ecumenism risks doctrinal compromise and prioritizes institutional unity over confessional distinctives.

American actor best known for playing Lou Grant on television. Asner won seven Primetime Emmy Awards, the most of any male performer, five of them for Lou Grant. He starred in the ABC sitcom *Thunder Alley* (1994–1995) and voiced Carl Fredricksen in the [[Pixar]] film *Up* (2009). He served in the U.S. Army Signal Corps during the [[Korean War]] from 1951 to 1953.

American murderer and body snatcher. In 1957, authorities discovered that Gein had stolen corpses from graveyards near his hometown of Plainfield, Wisconsin, and made keepsakes from their bones and skin. He confessed to killing two women, tavern owner Mary Hogan in 1954 and hardware store owner Bernice Worden in 1957. He was found guilty of Worden's murder but legally insane and committed to a psychiatric institution. His case inspired *Psycho* (1960) by [[Alfred Hitchcock]].

American actor and former [[American football|football]] player. O'Neill played Al Bundy, a working-class father, on the Fox sitcom *Married... with Children* (1987–1997). He later played the patriarch Jay Pritchett in the ABC sitcom *Modern Family* (2009–2020), where the ensemble won four Screen Actors Guild Awards. He was signed as an undrafted free agent by the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]] in 1969 but was cut in training camp.

English singer-songwriter. Sheeran has sold 200 million records worldwide. His album *÷* (*Divide*, 2017) was the best-selling album worldwide that year, and he was named Global Recording Artist of the Year. The single "Thinking Out Loud," from his second album, won two [[Grammy Awards]], including Song of the Year. In 2025, [[Time (magazine)|Time]] listed him among the world's 100 most influential people.

American paranormal investigators and authors. Ed Warren, a self-professed demonologist, and Lorraine Warren, who professed to be clairvoyant, founded the [[New England]] Society for Psychic Research in 1952. According to the Warrens, they investigated well over 10,000 cases, and their stories inspired dozens of films, including *The Conjuring* (2013). Skeptics Joe Nickell and Benjamin Radford concluded that the better-known Amityville and Snedeker hauntings did not happen and had been invented.

British stand-up comedian, actress and activist. Izzard's stand-up, known for rambling, whimsical monologues, includes the tour *Dress to Kill* (1998), for which Izzard won two Primetime Emmy Awards. In 2009 Izzard completed 43 [[Marathon|marathons]] in 51 days for Sport Relief, and in 2016 ran 27 marathons in 27 days in South Africa in honor of Nelson Mandela. Izzard is an active supporter of the [[European Union]] and a [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour Party]] activist.

American comedian, actor and singer. Born in [[Brooklyn]], Murphy rose to fame on [[Saturday Night Live]] (1980–1984) and then starred in films including *48 Hrs.* (1982), *Trading Places* (1983) and *Beverly Hills Cop* (1984). He voiced the donkey in the [[Shrek]] films and won a Golden Globe for Best Supporting Actor for *Dreamgirls* (2006). In 2020 he won his first Primetime Emmy Award.

English actor. Redmayne won an Academy Award for playing physicist [[Stephen Hawking]] in *The Theory of Everything* (2014) and was nominated for playing Lili Elbe in *The Danish Girl* (2015). Critics, including some [[Transgender|transgender]] activists, objected to casting a cisgender man as a transgender woman in that film. He won a Laurence Olivier Award for Best Actor in a Musical for *Cabaret* and played Newt Scamander in the *Fantastic Beasts* films.

[[Belgium|Belgian]] road and track cyclist widely regarded as the most successful rider in the history of competitive cycling. He won an unequaled eleven Grand Tours, including five [[Tour de France|Tours de France]], five Giros d'Italia and a Vuelta a España, along with all five Monuments, the major one-day classics. He won three World Championships and 525 victories over an eighteen-year career. In October 1972 he broke the hour record, extending it by almost 800 meters. Nicknamed "the Cannibal," he retired in 1978, later founded the bicycle brand Eddy Merckx Cycles in 1980, and coached the Belgian national team for eleven years.

Loop of electric current induced within conductors by a changing magnetic field, also called Foucault's current. Eddy currents flow in closed loops perpendicular to the magnetic field and arise from time-varying fields, as in an AC electromagnet or [[Transformer|transformer]], or from relative motion between a magnet and a conductor. By Lenz's law, an eddy current creates a field that opposes the change that produced it, so a nearby conductive surface drags on a moving magnet, a principle used in eddy current brakes. Their resistance also dissipates energy as heat, causing losses in transformers, [[Electric motor|motors]] and generators that laminated or ferrite cores reduce. Eddy currents also heat metal in induction furnaces and reveal cracks in metal parts through eddy-current testing. [[Léon Foucault]] is credited with discovering them in 1855.

American writer, poet and critic known for tales of mystery and the macabre. Poe was one of the central figures of [[Romanticism]] and [[Gothic fiction]] in the United States and of early American literature. He was among the country's first successful practitioners of the [[Short story|short story]] and is generally considered a pioneer of [[Detective fiction|detective fiction]], and he contributed significantly to the emergence of [[Science fiction|science fiction]]. He was the first well-known American writer to earn a living exclusively through writing, which resulted in a financially difficult life. His poem "[[The Raven]]" (1845) brought instant success, and he died in [[Baltimore]] under mysterious circumstances. His work influenced literature worldwide and fields such as [[Cryptography]].

French painter, draftsman and sculptor known for pastels and oil paintings of dancers and racehorses. Degas is regarded as one of the founders of [[Impressionism]], though he rejected the label and preferred to be called a realist. Born in [[Paris]], he is especially identified with dance, and more than half of his works depict dancers, many of them [[Ballet|ballet]] dancers. After academic training, he spent three years in [[Italy]] copying Renaissance masters, and he registered as a copyist at the [[Louvre]]. He also produced wax sculptures, prints and portraits notable for psychological complexity and human isolation, as well as paintings of racehorses and jockeys.

Third and last period of the Neoproterozoic Era, from 635 to 538.8 million years ago. It is named after the Ediacara Hills of South Australia, where geologist Reg Sprigg discovered trace fossils of the Ediacaran biota in 1946. The period marks the first widespread appearance of complex multicellular life after the [[Snowball Earth]] glaciation, and it ends at the beginning of the [[Cambrian]] Period, when recognizable [[Fossil|fossil]] evidence of life becomes common.

City (pop., 2020: 506,520), capital of [[Scotland]]. Edinburgh has been recognized as Scotland's capital since at least the 15th century and is the seat of the Scottish Government, the Scottish Parliament and the country's highest courts. It is Scotland's second-largest city, after [[Glasgow]], and is home to the University of Edinburgh, founded in 1582. Its Old Town and New Town, which includes the Georgian New Town built in the 18th and 19th centuries, are together a [[World Heritage Site]] listed by [[UNESCO]]. The city hosts the Edinburgh International Festival and the Fringe, which is the world's largest annual international arts festival.

American writer and designer. Wharton drew on her knowledge of upper-class New York society to portray the lives and morals of the [[Gilded Age]]. In 1921 she became the first woman to win the [[Pulitzer Prize]] for Fiction, for *The Age of Innocence*. Her other well-known works include *The House of Mirth*, the novella *Ethan Frome* and several ghost stories. She moved permanently to France in 1907, where she wrote design manuals and cultivated gardens, and she maintained a friendship with [[Henry James]]. Her literary output exceeded fifty volumes.

English astronomer, mathematician and physicist. From an observatory on [[Saint Helena]] in 1676–77, Halley cataloged the southern sky and recorded a transit of Mercury, and he realized that transits of Venus could be used to measure the distances between Earth, Venus and the Sun. Using [[Newton's law of universal gravitation]], he computed the periodicity of [[Halley's Comet]], predicting its return in 1758, which he did not live to see. Halley encouraged and helped fund the publication of [[Isaac Newton]]'s *Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica* (1687). He became the second Astronomer Royal in 1720, and in 1718 he discovered the proper motion of the fixed stars.

City (pop., 2021: 1,010,899), capital of [[Alberta]], Canada. Edmonton lies on the North Saskatchewan River and serves as a staging point for oil sands projects in northern Alberta and diamond mining in the [[Northwest Territories]]. Its trading post, Fort Edmonton, became the main center of trade in the area after the 1821 merger of the [[Hudson's Bay Company]] and the North West Company. The city is known as "Canada's Festival City" and is home to West Edmonton Mall, Canada's largest mall.

Anglo-Irish writer, philosopher and politician, widely credited as the founder of [[Conservatism|conservatism]]. He sat in the House of Commons from 1766 to 1794 as a member of the Whig Party, and in 1774 was elected for [[Bristol]]. In *Reflections on the Revolution in France* (1790), he argued that the [[French Revolution]] was destroying the traditional institutions of state and society, and he condemned the resulting persecution of the Catholic Church. He supported Catholic emancipation and the rights of the American colonists to resist British taxation, though he opposed their independence. He led the attempt to impeach Warren Hastings of the [[East India Company]] and argued against unrestricted power.

New Zealand mountaineer, explorer and philanthropist. On 29 May 1953, Hillary and [[Tenzing Norgay]] became the first climbers confirmed to reach the summit of [[Mount Everest]]. He reached the [[South Pole]] overland in 1958 during the Commonwealth Trans-Antarctic Expedition and later reached the [[North Pole]], becoming the first person to reach both poles and summit Everest. In 1960 he founded the Himalayan Trust to assist the Sherpa people of [[Nepal]], and his efforts are credited with building many schools and hospitals there. He had served as a navigator in the Royal New Zealand Air Force during [[World War II]], and from 1985 to 1988 he was New Zealand's High Commissioner to India and Bangladesh.

Austrian-German philosopher and mathematician who founded the school of [[Phenomenology (philosophy)|phenomenology]]. His early work critiqued historicism and psychologism in logic, based on analyses of intentionality. In his mature work he sought a systematic foundational science built on the phenomenological reduction, redefining phenomenology as a transcendental idealist philosophy. He received his doctorate in mathematics at Vienna in 1883 with a thesis on the [[Calculus of variations|calculus of variations]]. He taught at Halle, Göttingen and Freiburg, retiring in 1928. In 1933, under the racial laws of the [[Nazi Party]], he was banned from the university library at Freiburg because of his Jewish family background.

English poet, author of the epic *The Faerie Queene*. The work, an allegory celebrating the Tudor dynasty and [[Elizabeth I]], established Spenser as one of the premier craftsmen of Modern English verse. In 1580 he went to Ireland in the service of Lord Deputy Arthur Grey and acquired an estate at Kilcolman in North Cork. He also wrote the [[Sonnet|sonnet]] sequence *Amoretti* (1595) and *Epithalamion* (1595). His prose pamphlet *A View of the Present State of Irelande* (1596) argued that Ireland would not be pacified until its indigenous language and customs were destroyed, if necessary by violence. In 1598 he was driven from his home during the Nine Years' War, and he returned to London, where he was buried in [[Westminster Abbey]].

Period of Japanese history, from 1600 or 1603 to 1868, under the Tokugawa shogunate. [[Tokugawa Ieyasu]] prevailed at the [[Battle of Sekigahara]] in 1600 and took the title [[Shogun|shogun]] in 1603. The period was marked by prolonged peace, urbanization, economic growth and strict social order. Under the policy of *sakoku*, all foreigners were expelled by 1639 except Dutch traders confined to Dejima in [[Nagasaki]]. Merchants prospered, and [[Kabuki]] and [[Ukiyo-e]] flourished in Edo, [[Osaka]] and Kyoto. In 1853 Commodore Matthew C. Perry forced Japan to open to Western trade, and the period ended with the [[Meiji Restoration]] in 1868.

Dutch computer scientist, programmer and mathematician. In 1952 Dijkstra became the Netherlands' first programmer at the Mathematical Centre in [[Amsterdam]]. In 1956 he solved the shortest path problem, now known as [[Dijkstra's algorithm]], and in 1960 he developed the first compiler for ALGOL 60 with J. A. Zonneveld. He moved to Eindhoven in 1962 as a professor and built the THE multiprogramming system, whose software-based paged virtual memory influenced later systems. He joined Burroughs Corporation in 1973 and wrote nearly 500 documents in the "EWD" series. He taught at the University of Texas at Austin from 1984 until his retirement in 1999, and he received the 1972 ACM Turing Award for fundamental contributions to structured programming languages.
